title: Al-Fajr: the orphan, again
hook: no, you don't honor the orphan or urge feeding the poor, and you love wealth too much (89:17–20)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Fajr, and the tour of old cities, 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh. Your line was towers fall. What did you pass that was built to impress? Day one hundred ninety-seven.

Listen to how people talk when life goes well. I worked hard. I earned this. Things are finally going my way. And when it goes badly: why me? What did I do to deserve this? Both sound natural. Both are about me. Al-Fajr catches that exact habit, the one that reads every good day as a reward and every hard day as an insult, and then it does something sharp. It changes the subject to someone else entirely. Someone we've met before in these surahs, twice already. Today: the orphan, again.

Verses fifteen and sixteen describe the human being tested two ways. Given honor and comfort, he says: my Lord has honored me. Given a tight, narrow provision, he says: my Lord has humiliated me. Then verse seventeen, in Pickthall's words: "Nay, but ye (for your part) honour not the orphan." It's a turn of the tables. You think the question is whether God honors you. The surah asks whether you honor the one with no one. Then three more. You don't urge each other to feed the poor. You swallow up inheritance, greedily, and in that world the inheritance most often swallowed belonged to orphans and widows. And you love wealth with a love that has no bottom. This is the third time the orphan has appeared on this stretch of the path. In Ad-Duha: don't be harsh with the orphan. In Al-Balad: feed an orphan who's a relative, on a day of hunger. Now here. The Qur'an keeps returning to the orphan partly because the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was one. His father died before he was born; his mother when he was six. He was raised by a grandfather and then an uncle. A hadith in Bukhari says he held up two fingers, side by side, and said that he and the one who cares for an orphan will be in Paradise like this. Notice the word, too. Not feed or help. Honor, tukrimun, from the same root as karim, generous, noble. An orphan isn't a project. The surah asks for dignity, and it asks you to urge others toward it, not only to give quietly yourself.
screen: `HONORED, OR HUMILIATED?` · `YOU DON'T HONOR THE ORPHAN.` · `THE THIRD TIME ON THIS PATH.` · `HONOR, NOT ONLY HELP.` · then, large: `HONOR THE ORPHAN.`

segments.voice: Sit for two minutes and think of a child who has lost a parent. Maybe one you know, a friend's child, a student, a neighbor. Maybe one you'll never meet. Hold them in mind with respect, not pity. Then decide one thing: a gift to a charity that cares for orphans, a message to a family who's grieving, time with a child who needs a steady adult. The bell holds the time.
Al-Fajr. The dawn, Surah eighty-nine, which asks not whether God honors you, but whether you honor the orphan. Today's word.
Your line: honor the orphan. Do the one thing you chose, and if you can, tell one other person about it, so the urging spreads. Day one hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Caring for orphans is a long-standing Muslim practice: many sponsor an orphan through a charity, support orphanages, or take in relatives' children, recalling that the Prophet was himself an orphan.

fork.setup: a man says: my Lord has honored me, when life is good, and humiliated me, when it's hard. how does the surah answer?
options: it agrees: good times show God's favor
it turns to how he treats the orphan and the poor
it tells him to stop complaining
fork.reveal: Nay: you don't honor the orphan (89:17). the question shifts from how God treats you to how you treat the one with no one.

original.note: Arabic: the orphan, a child who has lost a father; the word also names a single, unmatched pearl.

trapdoor: what you thought: be kind to orphans.
what it means: stop reading your own fortune as God's verdict on you, and honor the orphan, urge feeding the poor, and loosen your grip on wealth.
what a scholar hears: kalla, the sharp "nay" of 89:17, turns the argument; the orphan appears in 93:9, 90:15 and 89:17, and the Prophet's own orphanhood (93:6) sits behind all three.
